title: Guru Gobind Singh's gurpurab
hook: his birth is celebrated in winter with kirtan and processions

segments.voice: Yesterday, the akhand path, the unbroken reading. Your line was unbroken. Today, another gurpurab, in the middle of winter.

A nurse who's gentle with patients and fierce with bad doctors. A grandmother who writes poetry and once faced down a landlord. People get sorted into boxes all the time: the soft ones, the tough ones. The tenth Guru fits in neither. His poetry fills much of the Sikh morning prayers, and he led armies into battle. Sikhs celebrate his birthday in the heart of winter: Guru Gobind Singh's gurpurab.
screen: `GENTLE AND FIERCE AT ONCE.` → `POET AND COMMANDER.` → `A BIRTHDAY IN WINTER.`

segments.voice: Guru Gobind Singh was born in 1666 in Patna, in eastern India, where a great gurdwara, one of the five Takhts, the seats of Sikh authority, now stands. His gurpurab falls in December or January, and it's kept the way you'd now expect: an akhand path, a nagar kirtan through the streets, kirtan and langar, and at Patna Sahib, pilgrims from far away. The exact date moves from year to year, and different Sikh calendars have calculated it differently; Sikhs have debated that, but not the celebration itself. Now the sword and the song. You've already met his words on this path: Jaap Sahib's galloping praise, the savaiyas that say without love, nothing, Chaupai asking to be kept under God's hand. He wrote in more than one language, and tradition says he kept poets at his court. He was also a military leader who fought many battles to defend his people, created the Khalsa, and lost his father and all four of his sons in those years of persecution. How do the two fit? Sikhs call the ideal sant sipahi: saint-soldier. Devotion first, and courage in its service. In a Persian letter to the emperor Aurangzeb, the Zafarnama, Guru Gobind Singh says, in paraphrase, that when every other means has failed, it is right to take up the sword. Every other means first. And there's a line from his Akal Ustat. In paraphrase: recognize the whole human race as one. That's the song the sword was meant to protect.
screen: `BORN IN PATNA, 1666.` · `A WINTER GURPURAB.` · `SANT SIPAHI — SAINT-SOLDIER.` · `THE WHOLE HUMAN RACE AS ONE.` · then, large: `SWORD AND SONG.`

segments.voice: Say his line silently and slowly, three times: recognize the whole human race as one. Then, for a few breaths, hold in that line one group of people you find hard to see as your own, whoever it is for you: not agreeing with everything, just human, one kind with you. If you pray, you can hold them before God.
Gurpurab. The Guru's remembrance day, kept in winter for the tenth Guru's birthday, with kirtan and processions: the poet-commander, sword and song.
Your line: sword and song. The tenth Guru held both. That's day one hundred forty-nine.

notes: Zafarnama line (chu kar az hama hilate dar guzasht, halal ast burdan ba shamsher dast) paraphrased. Confirm.
Akal Ustat line 'manas ki jat sabai ekai pahichanbo' (recognize the whole human race as one) paraphrased. Confirm.

Date: lunar Poh sudi 7; the original Nanakshahi calendar fixed January 5; the SGPC later returned to the lunar date, so some years have two or none. Summarized as 'different Sikh calendars have calculated it differently'. Confirm.
The practice asks the listener to hold 'a group you find hard to see as your own'; kept neutral. Confirm.
